may only lower, a key's quota may be raised or lowered by you: it protects the Bridge from its own callers, not a
broker from the Bridge. Every response carries `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers (IETF draft format).

**Bounds.** A quota (in the config, or set through the API) takes finite numbers from 0.01 to 10,000 requests a second (one
request every 100 seconds at the least), a burst of 1 to 100,000 (a whole number), 1 to 100,000,000 requests a day (or `null`
for no daily cap) and a weight of 1 to 16. Anything else, including `NaN`, a negative number, a string or a rate like `1e-7`
that would lock a key out for months, is refused. The **only active admin key** may not be given less than 1 request a second
and 1,000 a day: a quota applies to the key, so one that is too small could lock you out of the API. **If a key is ever locked
out**, this computer's control token is not subject to any quota: run `mc-bridge` on this computer (the dashboard opened with
`mc-bridge open` works too) and delete the override (`DELETE /v1/quotas/<keyId>` as a local caller), or edit or remove
`quotas.json` in the data folder while the Bridge is stopped.

## Asking for less: stale-while-revalidate and prefetch priority

- `?swr=true` on `/v1/ltp`, `/v1/quotes` and `/v1/optionchain`: when only an older cached value exists (inside
  `market.stale.maxStaleMs`), it answers at once with `freshness.stale: true` and `freshness.revalidating: true`, and one
  refresh runs behind it (however many readers ask). The next read gets the fresh value from the cache.
- `?priority=background`: a prefetch. It waits behind every interactive read; a person's click on the same thing joins
  it and raises its priority. The dashboard prefetches this way when you hover a menu item or an expiry chip.

## Seeing it work

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/limits                 # effective policy per broker, your key's budget
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/limits?explain=1"     # + the shared pools and who is waiting
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/usage                  # per account and class: used, queued, back-off; savings
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/usage?series=1"       # + calls per second over the last two minutes
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/usage?view=budget"    # the dashboard's budget summary
```

`savings` counts the broker calls avoided today: served from stream, served from cache, coalesced and batched. Each
class lists every window (`windows`: this second, this minute, today) with what it holds now. Admin keys also get
`consumers`: today's broker calls and saved calls per dashboard page, API key (by label), MCP, Excel / compat and
background jobs.

`explain=1` adds, in numbers instead of log lines, why a request may have been slow or refused: `pools` (each budget
pool's accounts, spare room, ceiling, current scale and back-off, throttles in the last hour) and `consumers` (who is
queued or in flight and each one's share), plus `you`, your own key's quota and use. Other keys appear only to admin keys.

The dashboard shows the same figures. The **API** capsule in the top bar shows this second and this minute against the
limit, the stream and the calls saved today (fed by `budget` messages on the stream, op `subscribe_budget`). The
**Sources** page has the rest: **Overview** (how each source and account is doing, recent requests with what answered
each one, and a "Why this source?" check), **Providers** (switch sources on and off, keys, notices) and **Quotas** (each
key's share, with presets and usage). Recent requests are also `GET /v1/requests` on this computer; a market read there
carries `route`, a short record of what answered it (stream, cache, a shared call, a live call, or a stale value, with the
source, its data class and delay).

---

<!-- docs/guides/sources.md -->

# Data sources: where prices come from, and how the Bridge labels them

Your broker accounts are the Bridge's main source of market data. They give real-time prices and option chains, and they
are the only sources that orders, risk checks, paper fills and alerts use. The Bridge can also read from optional free
sources and from plugins you add. Those are slower or less certain, so every answer from them says so.

This guide is for people who use the Bridge. If you are writing a source, read [source-contract.md](../source-contract.md).

## What you get from each kind of source

| Kind | What it is | Is it on? |
|---|---|---|
| **Your broker accounts** (`builtin`) | Real-time prices, option chains, history, from your own login | Always on |
| **Bring your own key** (`byok`) | A data vendor where you hold the account and paste its API key | Off until you save a key and turn it on |
| **Opt-in** (`opt-in`) | Works without a key, but is unofficial or has strict terms | Off until you read a notice and say yes |
| **Plugin** (`plugin`) | Code someone else wrote, that you reviewed and approved | Off until you approve it |

There is no free, official source of real-time Indian market data that you may redistribute. Real-time prices and option
chains come from your broker. The other sources are for history, for a second opinion on a price, and for filling in
when no broker account can answer. They are labelled `delayed` or `eod` and are never mixed into a real-time answer.

## What the labels mean

Every price, candle and option chain the Bridge returns says where it came from. In the API this is the `freshness`
object; the dashboard shows the same words on a badge.

```json
"freshness": {
  "source": "backup",
  "provider": "yahoo",
  "asOf": "2026-10-19T09:45:00+05:30",
  "ageMs": 61000,
  "stale": false,
  "class": "delayed",
  "delaySec": 900,
  "official": false,
  "confidence": "low",
  "flags": ["unofficial", "delayed"]
}
```

| Label | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| `class: "realtime"` | From your own broker, or its live feed. Safe to act on. |
| `class: "delayed"` | The source is slow by nature, usually about 15 minutes. `delaySec` says how many seconds. The price is a real price from the past. |
| `class: "eod"` | End of day. You get yesterday's close, not today's price. |
| `official: false` | Not a documented API from the data's owner. It may change or stop without notice, and its terms may not allow what you do with it. |
| `confidence` | `high` for broker data. Lower for delayed, end-of-day, unofficial or flagged data. |
| `flags` | Extra warnings, for example `unofficial`, `delayed`, `eod`, `plugin`, `last-bar-provisional` (the newest candle is still forming). |
| `stale: true` | The value is older than the freshness target for that read. This is separate from delayed. |

**Delayed is not the same as stale.** A quote from a 15-minute source is `delayed`. It is not `stale` if you asked for
data that old. A broker quote that is two minutes old when you wanted two seconds is `stale` but still `realtime`.

**One value comes from one source, with one timestamp.** The Bridge never fills a missing bid from another source or
averages two sources. An option chain or a many-symbol quote takes the least current class of its parts, so one delayed
leg makes the whole chain `delayed`.

Excel and Google Sheets formulas see only the body of the answer, not headers, so the label is always in the body.

## Turning a source on

You need an admin key, or the dashboard.

**On the dashboard:** open Sources, then Providers. Each source shows what it gives, its limits, its terms and its
health. Turn it on there. For a source that needs a key, paste the key first. For an opt-in source, read the notice; saying
yes records the notice version and the time.

**From the command line:**

```sh
mc-bridge sources list                       # what exists, what is on, how each is labelled
mc-bridge sources set-key twelvedata         # asks for the key with hidden input (or reads it from stdin)
mc-bridge sources test twelvedata            # one small call to check the key and the vendor
mc-bridge sources enable twelvedata          # byok: needs the key first
mc-bridge sources enable yahoo               # opt-in: prints the notice and does nothing yet
mc-bridge sources enable yahoo --acknowledge yahoo-1   # after you read it: the version printed above
mc-bridge sources disable yahoo
```

`set-key` takes only the source id. A key typed after it (`set-key twelvedata MYKEY`) is refused, because it would sit in your
shell history. Commands that need an admin key read `MCB_ADMIN_KEY` (or `MCB_API_KEY`) from the environment; `--key <key>` still
works but prints a warning for the same reason.

Keys are never taken from the command line, so they do not end up in your shell history. They are stored encrypted on this
computer, never written to `bridge.config.json`, and never shown again, not even by the API.

If the notice changes, its version changes and you are asked again.

## The built-in sources

| Source | Kind | Gives | Limits the Bridge keeps to | Read this first |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yahoo Finance | opt-in | Delayed quotes and history | 1 a second, 60 a minute | Unofficial. Yahoo's terms restrict automated access, so use it only for your own cross-checks. |
| Alpha Vantage | byok | End-of-day history and quotes | 5 a minute, 25 a day on the free key | Daily data only; intraday needs a paid plan. |
| Twelve Data | byok | End-of-day history and quotes | 8 a minute, 800 a day | Indian exchange data needs a paid plan; a free key is refused for Indian symbols. |

The numbers are the vendors' documented limits (or conservative figures where a vendor publishes none). The Bridge never
asks for more. Each notice shows the vendor's terms link and what you accept; the dashboard shows it before you turn a
source on. You are responsible for having the right to use a vendor's data.

In demo mode the Bridge also offers `demo-delayed` and `demo-eod` with sample data, so you can see every label without
a real source.

## When the Bridge uses a source

For a read that is not pinned to one account, the Bridge looks at the candidates and picks one:

1. It drops sources that cannot do the job: wrong capability, data too old for what you asked (`maxAgeMs`), not allowed for
   the purpose, circuit breaker open.
2. It prefers the candidate with the most spare budget, the lowest error rate and the lowest latency. It tries at most two
   candidates per request, so a failover is the retry.
3. Your live stream and the freshness cache are always tried first. Sources only add candidates; they never skip the cache.

**Purposes.** A read may say what it is for with `purpose`: `display` (default), `analysis`, `alert`, `paper`, `risk` or
`order`. The last four accept only real-time data from your own broker. A delayed or end-of-day source is never used for
them, whatever you configured, and neither is a cached value that has gone stale. Orders go through the account they belong to;
no source ever influences that.

The default, `display`, is for the public market routes: a `display` read may be answered from a cached value that is older
than its freshness target (labelled `stale: true`) when your broker's budget is used up, and from a backup source if the read
allows one. So code inside the Bridge never relies on the default. The order service (price band, market protection, strike
choice) reads with `purpose: "order"`, the paper engine with `"paper"`, and both check the label on what comes back: a value
that is stale, delayed, end of day, unofficial, from a source or unlabelled is not used as a price. A test scans the order,
paper, safety and compat code and fails if a market-data call there does not state its purpose.

**`maxAgeMs`.** If you ask for data no older than 2 seconds, a 15-minute source cannot answer, and you get your broker's
answer or an error, not a delayed price pretending to be fresh.

**Fallback.** When no broker account can answer (all logged out, all at their limit), the Bridge can answer from an
enabled source instead, but only if you allow it: the switch "Use free sources automatically when my brokers cannot
answer" on Sources > Providers (saved by the Bridge; `PATCH /v1/sources/settings`), `"sources": { "autoFallback": true }`
in the config, or `backup=true` on one request. The switch, once used, wins over the config. It is off by default. The answer carries the labels above, so you can tell.

A source that keeps failing is paused for a while (the Sources page says "Paused" and when it will be tried again),
and tried again after a cooldown that grows up to five minutes. A rate-limit answer, a bad key or an unknown symbol does
not pause it. A plugin that crashes is shown with its own reason.

To see why a source was or was not used, ask for a trace. It is a dry run: nothing is fetched.

```sh
mc-bridge sources trace --capability quotes --symbols NSE:RELIANCE --purpose display
```

```
Request: quotes NSE:RELIANCE, purpose display

CHOSEN    dhan-main              best spare budget (score 0.91, spare 0.8)
SKIPPED   yahoo                  delayed data cannot meet maxAgeMs 2000

Class of the answer: realtime. Served by your broker.
This was a dry run: no source was called.
```

## Seeing what answered a request

On the Sources page, **Overview** lists recent requests with a line for each: "answered from Dhan", "served from cache",
"used Yahoo, delayed 15 min". The same record is on `GET /v1/requests` (this computer only) as `route`:
`from` (`stream`, `cache`, `shared`, `live` or `stale`), the source and its name, the data class and the delay. For a
read of many symbols it is a summary, the least current verdict, never a list per symbol. The answer to the request
itself carries the full `freshness` label.

## How pooling and quotas fit

- **Pooling** spreads read-only market-data calls over your own accounts of one holder. It is separate from sources, off by
  default, and needs your consent (`GET /v1/pooling`, or the Sources page) because no broker's published terms clearly
  allow it. It never touches orders. See [rate-limits.md](rate-limits.md).
- **Source budgets.** Each source has its own budget from its documented limits, kept apart from your broker budgets. A
  free source never uses up your broker's request allowance, and a broker 429 does not slow a source.
- **Quotas.** Each API key has its own request quota and a weight in the queue, so one runaway spreadsheet cannot starve an
  AI assistant. A refusal says which limit tripped (`scope`: `client`, `upstream`, `queue` or `consumer-cap`) and when to
  try again. The dashboard (Sources, Quotas) and `GET /v1/quotas` show every key's share. `GET /v1/limits?explain=1` shows
  the shared pools and who is waiting.

## Plugins

A plugin is a read-only data source written by someone else, for example a vendor the Bridge has no built-in support for.
A plugin can answer quote, history, expiry and option-chain questions. It cannot place orders, log in, or see your
accounts, balances, positions or keys. Its data is always labelled `delayed` or `eod`, `official: false`, with the flag
`plugin`.

Treat a plugin as code you run on your computer, because it is. The Bridge limits what it can do:

- it runs in its own process with an empty environment, so it sees none of the Bridge's settings or secrets;
- all of its network access goes through the Bridge, and only to the https hosts its manifest lists and you approved;
- its files are pinned by hash, and a changed file is refused until you approve the change;
- it has call timeouts and request limits, and is stopped if it misbehaves.

These limits are real but not a complete sandbox. Node.js cannot stop a determined plugin from opening its own network
connection, and **a plugin runs as your user, so it can also send signals to the Bridge, for example kill it** (no setting
inside the Bridge can block that). Only use plugins whose code you have read or whose author you trust. If you must run one you
trust less, run it as another user (see "Running plugins as another user" below) or inside a container. [source-contract.md](../source-contract.md)
explains exactly what is and is not enforced.

To add one, in this order:

1. **Read** `mc-source.json` and the entry file (`index.mjs`). The folder may not contain symbolic links; the Bridge refuses it if it does.
2. **Pin** it: `mc-bridge sources plugins pin ./my-plugin` prints what you would grant (the hosts it may reach, its limits, its
   terms, the two files to read) and the pin.
3. Optionally **check** it: `mc-bridge sources plugins check ./my-plugin` runs its conformance checks offline. **`check` runs the
   plugin's code** on your computer (in the same restricted process and with a scripted network, but it is still its code), which
   is why it comes after you have read the files and pinned them, not before.

Then add it to the config:

```json
"sources": {
  "plugins": [
    { "path": "./my-plugin", "sha256": "<the pin>", "granted": true }
  ]
}
```

**Running plugins as another user.** If the Bridge runs as root on Linux or macOS (for example in a container or a service), you
can start every plugin as an unprivileged user so it cannot signal or kill the Bridge:

```json
"sources": { "pluginUser": { "uid": 1500, "gid": 1500 } }
```

The user must be able to read the plugin's folder. It is optional and never required. If it is set and the Bridge may not switch
user (it does not run as root, or the system is Windows), the plugins are **not started** and the log says why; they are never
quietly started with the Bridge's own privileges. A plugin is also never run as root. A plain desktop install runs as your own
user and cannot do this.

**If the Bridge was killed.** When the Bridge stops normally, on Ctrl+C or on a termination signal, it stops its plugin processes.
A forced kill of the Bridge (`kill -9`, the task manager's "end task", the out-of-memory killer) cannot clean up, and a plugin
stuck in a busy loop does not notice its connection closing, so it can keep running and using CPU. Find and stop it:

```sh
pgrep -af "plugin/child.mjs"      # Linux and macOS: lists the plugin processes
kill <pid>                        # then kill -9 <pid> if it stays
```

On Windows, look in Task Manager for `node.exe` processes whose command line contains `plugin\child.mjs`.

A plugin may have settings of its own; put them in a `config` object on its entry (the plugin's manifest says which keys
it takes, and a bad value stops it from loading). Never put a key there: a plugin's API key is saved from the Providers
tab like any other.

Restart the Bridge, then turn the plugin on like any other source. A plugin you granted but did not switch on is listed
as off. If you or anyone edits the plugin later, the Bridge
refuses it until you run `pin` again and update the line. A plugin that crashes four times in ten minutes is switched off,
and the reason shows in its health on the Sources page.

**Acknowledgements for opt-in sources.** Switching an opt-in source on needs you to acknowledge its notice. If you switch it off and
on again within 24 hours, one click is enough. If it has been off for more than 24 hours, or its notice changed, the notice is
shown again and the new acknowledgement is recorded (`needsAcknowledgement` in `GET /v1/sources` says which). At start, the Bridge
checks every source its state file marks as on: an opt-in source with no acknowledgement for the current notice is treated as off,
and a warning in the log names it. Those files (`sources/state.json`, the secrets store, the config) are **trusted local state, not
tamper-proof**: anyone who can write to the Bridge's data folder can change them, and the checks catch an honest mistake or a
restored backup, not a determined person.

## Configuration

```json
"sources": {
  "autoFallback": false,
  "timeoutMs": 5000,
  "pluginUser": { "uid": 1500, "gid": 1500 },
  "providers": { "yahoo": { "enabled": false } },
  "plugins": [{ "path": "./my-plugin", "sha256": "<the pin>", "granted": true, "config": {} }]
}
```

`pluginUser` is optional (see above). `autoFallback` is off unless you set it. `timeoutMs` is how long one call to a source may take (100 to 15000, 5000 by
default). `"enabled": false` under `providers` keeps a source off whatever the dashboard says. Whether a source is on, and the notices you acknowledged, are kept by the Bridge in
its data folder; use the dashboard or `mc-bridge sources` to change them. Keys are not config.

## Questions

**Why is a price 15 minutes old?** It came from a delayed source and the label says so (`class: "delayed"`). Real-time
prices come only from your broker. Log in to your broker account on the Accounts page.

**Can I use a delayed or end-of-day price for an order or an alert?** No. Orders, risk checks, paper fills and alerts accept
only real-time data from your own broker. This is enforced where the Bridge picks a source, and again by plugins refusing
those reads.

**Can I average a broker price and a free source to be safe?** The Bridge does not, and you should not. They are prices
from different moments. The Bridge keeps one value, one source, one timestamp.

**Why is Yahoo off by default?** It is unofficial and its terms restrict automated use. The Bridge makes you read that
before it is turned on. Treat what it returns as a cross-check, not as a price to trade on.

**Does a source use my broker's request limit?** No. Each source has its own budget.

**Is there a free real-time source?** Not one the Bridge can offer. Official real-time Indian market data is licensed. Use
your broker's.

**Where is my API key stored?** In the Bridge's encrypted secrets store on this computer, under the source's name. It is
never in the config file, never in logs, and never returned by the API.

**Can a plugin see my broker password or place an order?** No. It runs without the Bridge's environment or files, and its
protocol has no way to ask for accounts or orders. Order code never imports plugin code, and a test checks that.

**Can I pass this data to other people?** The Bridge is for your own use. Broker and vendor terms generally forbid passing
market data on, and the Bridge does not redistribute it. If you plan to share anything built on this data, get advice on
exchange data rules first.

**How do I see what a source did?** `mc-bridge sources list` shows health and last error; `mc-bridge sources test <id>` makes
one call; `mc-bridge sources trace` explains a routing decision.

---

<!-- docs/guides/paper-margin.md -->

# Paper margin: how the Bridge estimates it

**Approximate, not the exchange's SPAN.** The paper engine, the order preview and the margin route all use one function,
`portfolioMargin()` in `server/bridge/calc/span-margin.js`, so they always agree. Your broker's figure is the one that counts for live orders.

## What it does

Legs are grouped by underlying (NIFTY, BANKNIFTY, RELIANCE …). Within a group, longs, shorts and futures offset each
other, which is where a hedge earns its benefit.

1. **Scan risk.** Every leg is revalued one day ahead under 16 scenarios:
   - the underlying moves 0, ±⅓, ±⅔ and ±1 of the price scan range (index 9 %, stock 15 %), each with volatility up and
     down 25 % of the leg's own IV;
   - two extreme moves of twice the range, counted at 35 %.

   Options use Black-76 at the leg's IV (implied from its price), futures move one for one. The scan risk is the worst
   loss over the grid.
2. **Premium.** Option buys pay their premium. The premium already covers a long's loss up to its current value, so
   the scan charge is the scan risk less the current value of the longs (never below zero).
3. **Exposure.** Index 2 %, stock 3.5 % of the notional of short options and futures.
4. **Calendar.** Legs in more than one expiry pay 1 % (index) or 2 % (stock) of the delta one expiry offsets against
   another.
5. **Expiry day.** Legs expiring today are scanned on their own (no offset against later expiries), and short index
   options expiring today carry 2 % extra (ELM).

Without a price for the underlying, its legs fall back to the simple per-leg model (premium for buys, 15 % of strike
value for option sells, 15 % of contract value for futures) and the API lists them in `fallback`.

## Examples (NIFTY at 26344, lot 65, 3 November expiry, demo prices)

| Position | Old per-leg model | Portfolio model |
|---|---|---|
| Short 26150 PE, 1 lot | ₹2.55L | ₹1.63L |
| Iron condor 25950 / 26150 PE, 26550 / 26750 CE | ₹5.33L | ₹87k (premium ₹19k, exposure ₹68k) |
| The same four legs, each on its own (`standalone`) | | ₹3.44L |

## Where you see it

- **Order preview:** `margin.required` is what the order adds to the paper account's book (a hedge can add 0).
- **API:** `POST /v1/paper/accounts/{accountId}/margin` with `{ legs: [{ symbol, side, lots, price? }] }` answers
  `before`, `after`, `change`, `alone`, `standalone`, a breakdown and the method. Nothing is placed.

## Settings

`paper.margin.model` is `"portfolio"` (default) or `"simple"` (every leg on its own with `futuresPct` and
`optionSellPct`, the model before October 2026). Equity, MCX and CDS always use the percentages.

## What it does not model

Real SPAN risk arrays from the exchange, inter-commodity spread credits (for example NIFTY against BANKNIFTY), the
short-option minimum charge, delivery margins in the expiry week of stock options, and broker-specific add-ons.

---

<!-- docs/guides/compat-api.md -->

# Compat REST and WebSocket API (`/api/v1`)

Many Indian algo tools, SDKs, AmiBroker and Excel add-ins and alert bridges speak one common REST style: `POST` a
JSON body to `/api/v1/<endpoint>` with the API key in the body as `apikey`, and read `{ "status": "success", ... }`
or `{ "status": "error", "message": ... }` back. The Bridge speaks it too, on its own port, so those tools can use
all your broker accounts with the Bridge's rate limiting and safety in between.

Point the tool at `http://127.0.0.1:4300` and give it a **Bridge API key** as its API key:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/api/v1/quotes -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "apikey": "mcb_...", "symbol": "RELIANCE", "exchange": "NSE" }'
```

## Symbols

Compact trading symbols with an exchange code: `RELIANCE` / `NSE`, `NIFTY` / `NSE_INDEX`, `SENSEX` / `BSE_INDEX`,
`NIFTY27OCT2625000CE` / `NFO`, `NIFTY27OCT26FUT` / `NFO`. Products: `CNC`, `MIS` (Bridge `INTRADAY`), `NRML` (Bridge
`MARGIN`). Price types: `MARKET`, `LIMIT`, `SL`, `SL-M`. History intervals: `1m 3m 5m 10m 15m 30m 1h D W M`, dates
`YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Endpoints

| Group | Endpoints |
|---|---|
| Account | `ping`, `funds`, `orderbook`, `tradebook`, `positionbook`, `holdings`, `analyzer`, `analyzer/toggle` |
| Orders | `placeorder`, `placesmartorder` (towards `position_size`), `basketorder`, `splitorder` (`splitsize`), `modifyorder`, `cancelorder`, `cancelallorder`, `closeposition`, `orderstatus`, `openposition`, `optionsorder` (by `offset` ATM / ITMn / OTMn) |
| Market data | `quotes`, `multiquotes`, `depth`, `history`, `intervals` |
| Instruments | `symbol`, `search`, `expiry`, `optionchain`, `optionsymbol` |
| Margin | `margin` (up to 50 `positions`; the same calculation as `POST /v1/margin/basket`) |

Compat answers have no field that says how current a price is, so they are **never built from a backup data source**
(Yahoo, a plugin, ...): the market-data and instrument endpoints read from your broker accounts only, whatever
`sources.autoFallback` says, and choosing a strike for `optionsorder` reads with the `order` purpose (trusted real-time data
only). When your broker is out of request budget, a recent cached value may still answer; in that rare case the `data` of a
quote carries `"stale": true`. Use the `/v1` routes when you want labelled backup data.

`margin` takes `positions` (`symbol`, `exchange`, `action`, `product`, `pricetype`, `quantity`, `price`) and answers `total_margin_required`, `span_margin`, `exposure_margin`, `hedge_benefit` and `source` (`broker` or `paper-model`, the approximate paper model) as numbers; see [alert-orders.md](alert-orders.md). Every endpoint is in [openapi.yaml](../openapi.yaml) under "Compat REST".

## Which account

Calls act on `compat.account` from the config, or else the first account the key may use. A Bridge extension: add
`"account": "<id>"` to any request body to pick another (the key must be allowed to use it).

## Orders are paper until you say otherwise

The Bridge starts every key in **analyzer mode**: orders are paper orders (replies carry `"mode": "analyze"`). To
send live orders:

1. turn live trading on the Bridge way: `safety.liveTrading`, the account's `live.enabled` with `"rest"` in
   `allowedSources` (see [safety.md](safety.md));
2. use a key with the `live` scope;
3. call `analyzer/toggle` with `{ "mode": false }`.

Every order still goes through the Bridge's validation, idempotency, safety limits, kill switch and audit log, and
data reads through its rate-limit engine. Market-data calls need a `read` key; order calls a `paper` (or `live`) key.

## WebSocket

`ws://127.0.0.1:4300/api/v1/ws`

```json
{ "action": "authenticate", "api_key": "mcb_..." }
{ "action": "subscribe", "mode": "Quote", "symbols": [{ "exchange": "NSE", "symbol": "RELIANCE" }, { "exchange": "NSE_INDEX", "symbol": "NIFTY" }] }
{ "action": "unsubscribe", "symbols": [{ "exchange": "NSE", "symbol": "RELIANCE" }] }
{ "action": "unsubscribe_all" }
```

Modes: `LTP` (1), `Quote` (2), `Depth` (3). Ticks arrive as
`{ "type": "market_data", "symbol", "exchange", "mode", "data": { "ltp", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume", "oi", "bid", "ask", "timestamp" } }`.
Authenticate within 15 seconds. All clients share one upstream feed per broker account.

## Settings

```json
"compat": { "enabled": true, "account": "dhan-main", "analyzer": true }
```

<!-- docs/guides/streaming.md -->

# Live streaming: WebSocket and SSE

One port serves both. Messages are described in [asyncapi.yaml](../asyncapi.yaml). This page is about prices; for events (orders,
logins, downloads, the kill switch) with replay and signed webhooks, see [events.md](events.md).

## Authenticate without putting your key in a URL

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/stream/token
# {"data":{"token":"...","expiresAt":"..."}}
```

The token is single use and must be used within 60 seconds; the connection then lives on with the key's scopes. A
client that can send headers may use `Authorization: Bearer` on the upgrade request instead. Revoking the key closes
its open connections at once.

## WebSocket

```js
const ws = new WebSocket(`ws://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/stream?token=${encodeURIComponent(token)}`);
ws.onopen = () => {
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: "subscribe", symbols: ["NSE:NIFTY", "NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-25000-CE"], mode: "quote", id: "s1" }));
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: "subscribe_orders", accounts: ["paper"] }));
};
ws.onmessage = (e) => {
  const m = JSON.parse(e.data);
  if (m.type === "snapshot") console.log("latest known", m.ticks);
  if (m.type === "tick") console.log(m.seq, m.symbol, m.ltp);
  if (m.type === "order") console.log(m.order.orderId, m.order.status);
  if (m.type === "go_away") console.log("reconnect after", m.reconnectAfterMs, m.reason);
};
```

| Client op | Effect |
|---|---|
| `subscribe` `{ symbols, mode: "ltp"\|"quote"\|"depth", id? }` | Answered with a `snapshot`, then `tick`s |
| `unsubscribe` `{ symbols }` | Stops those symbols for this connection |
| `subscribe_orders` `{ accounts? }` / `unsubscribe_orders` | Order updates for accounts the key may use |
| `ping` | Answered with a `heartbeat` |

Server messages: `heartbeat` (first message and every 15 s), `snapshot`, `tick`, `order`, `status` (a broker feed went
`up`, `stale` or `down`), `error`, `go_away`.

## SSE

```
GET /v1/stream/sse?token=<token>&symbols=NSE:NIFTY,NSE:RELIANCE&mode=ltp&orders=1
```

Same messages as the WebSocket; each event's `id` is its `seq`.

**Reconnects.** A browser's `EventSource` reconnects to the same URL by itself after a network blip. The token that
opened the stream may reopen that exact URL (same `symbols`, `mode` and `orders`) for up to 5 minutes after the
connection dropped, one open connection at a time, while the key is still valid. After that, or if you change the
URL, fetch a new token:

```js
async function openStream(symbols) {
  const r = await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/stream/token", { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}` } });
  const { data } = await r.json();
  const es = new EventSource(`http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/stream/sse?token=${encodeURIComponent(data.token)}&symbols=${symbols}`);
  es.addEventListener("tick", (e) => console.log(JSON.parse(e.data)));
  // readyState CLOSED means the browser gave up (for example the grace period ran out): start again with a fresh token.
  es.onerror = () => {
    if (es.readyState === EventSource.CLOSED) setTimeout(() => openStream(symbols), 3000);
  };
  return es;
}
```

## Behaviour worth knowing

- **One broker subscription per symbol per account**, shared by every client; dropped when the last client leaves.
- **Caps:** per connection (`stream.maxSymbolsPerClient`, 500), per request (200), total connections (50), connections
  per API key (`stream.maxClientsPerKey`, 10), and each
  broker's feed limit. Crossing one returns `SUBSCRIPTION_LIMIT` naming exactly the refused symbols.
- **Slow clients:** ticks wait in one slot per symbol; a newer tick replaces an older one (a gap in `seq` shows that,
  and the heartbeat counts conflated ticks). Other messages queue up to `stream.maxQueuedMessages`; a client that
  overflows gets `go_away` `slow_consumer`. Memory per client is bounded.
- **Reconnects:** if a broker feed drops, the Bridge reconnects with jittered back-off and resubscribes everything.
- Streaming makes REST reads cheaper too: a streamed symbol is served from the stream with no broker call.

---

<!-- docs/guides/events.md -->

# Events out: react to the Bridge without polling

The Bridge can tell your own programs when something happens: an order was filled, a broker login ended, a data download
finished, the kill switch was turned on. You can listen live (a stream), ask for what you missed (replay), or have the Bridge
call your program (a signed webhook).

Events are **notifications only**. They tell you what happened. Nothing you receive can place, change, confirm or reject an
order, and nothing that comes back from your program is read. An event never carries an API key, a signing secret or an
order-approval token. Approving an order stays on this computer, in the Bridge. Prices are not events: use the
[price stream](streaming.md) for those.

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| A script or app that is running now | [SSE or WebSocket](#listen-live-sse-and-websocket) |
| A script that runs now and then and wants what it missed | [Replay with a cursor](#cursors-and-replay) |
| The Bridge to call your server | [A webhook](#webhooks-the-bridge-calls-you) |

## Listen live: SSE and WebSocket

Both give the same events. Credentials are the same as for the price stream: a single-use token from
`POST /v1/stream/token`, or an `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header from a script. A read key is enough.

```bash
# every event your key may see, as it happens (Ctrl+C to stop)
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/events/stream"

# only orders and downloads, and everything kept since cursor 1000
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/events/stream?topics=order.*,download.*&since=1000"
```

Each SSE event looks like this (`id` is the cursor, `event` is the topic, `data` is the envelope):

```
id: 1043
event: order.updated
data: {"id":"1043","topic":"order.updated","time":"2026-11-09T04:01:02.000Z","apiVersion":"v1","data":{"orderId":"PAPER-20261109-0003","accountId":"paper","mode":"paper","status":"filled","filledQuantity":65,"avgPrice":182.4,"source":"rest"}}
```

In a browser page (the page's address must be on `cors.allowedOrigins`):

```js
const { data } = await (await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/stream/token", { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}` } })).json();
const es = new EventSource(`http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/events/stream?token=${encodeURIComponent(data.token)}&topics=order.*`);
es.addEventListener("ready", (e) => console.log("connected", JSON.parse(e.data)));
es.addEventListener("order.updated", (e) => console.log(JSON.parse(e.data).data));
```

`EventSource` reconnects by itself after a network blip and sends `Last-Event-ID`; the Bridge treats it as `since`, so
you get what you missed. The token that opened the stream may reopen that same URL for 5 minutes after the connection
dropped, one connection at a time.

WebSocket: `ws://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/events/ws?token=<token>&topics=order.*&since=<cursor>`. Frames are JSON:
`{"type":"ready",...}`, then `{"type":"event","id":"1043","topic":"order.updated","time":"...","apiVersion":"v1","data":{...}}`,
and `{"type":"go_away",...}` before a close. The only thing a client may send is `{"op":"ping"}`, answered with `{"type":"pong"}`.

Query parameters (both transports, and `GET /v1/events`):

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `topics` | Comma-separated filters: a topic (`order.updated`), a prefix (`order.*`) or `*` (the default) |
| `since` | A cursor. Replay the kept events after it, then go live. `0` is everything kept. Without it the stream is live only |
| `accounts` | Only events about these accounts. A key never sees more than its own accounts, whatever it asks for |

The first message is `ready`: `{ cursor, oldest, replayed, gap, gapReason, topics }`. `cursor` is the newest event now.

## Cursors and replay

Every event has a number, its **cursor**, counting up for as long as the Bridge's event file lives. Treat it as opaque and give
it back as `since` (or let `EventSource` do it).

- The last **5000** events (`events.retain`) are kept on disk in the data folder (`events/log.jsonl`) and survive a restart; the
  numbering continues, so a cursor from before the restart still works.
- If you ask for a cursor older than the oldest kept event, or newer than anything this Bridge has, you are told: `gap: true`
  with `gapReason` `retention` or `cursor_ahead`. You are still sent everything that is kept. Treat a gap as "read the current
  state from the API again" (orders, positions), then carry on from the new cursor.
- `GET /v1/events?since=1000&limit=100` is the same replay as one JSON answer, for a script that runs now and then.
  `meta.cursor` is what to ask with next time. Without `since` it returns the newest events.
- Noisy topics are thinned: `download.progress`, `stream.status` and `limits.throttled` keep at most one event per job or
  account per second.

```bash
cursor=0
while true; do
  r=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/events?since=$cursor&topics=order.*")
  echo "$r" | jq -c '.data[]'
  cursor=$(echo "$r" | jq -r '.meta.cursor')
  sleep 5
done
```

## Which events, and who sees them

`GET /v1/events/topics` lists what your key may receive. A **read** key sees the topics marked read. **Admin-only** topics
(order tickets, webhook alert problems, backups, config warnings) need an admin key. A key limited to some accounts only
receives events about those accounts; events that name no account (the kill switch, downloads) go to every key.

| Topic | Who | When |
|---|---|---|
| `order.updated` | read | An order (paper or live) changed state: `orderId`, `accountId`, `mode`, `status`, `filledQuantity`, `avgPrice`, `source` |
| `order.outcome_unknown` | read | The broker did not confirm an order. Check the broker before sending it again |
| `position.converted` | read | A position was moved between products |
| `account.status` | read | A broker login changed: `connected`, `expired`, `missing`, `error` |
| `account.login_needed` | read | Morning reminder: an account needs a login before the open |
| `trading.readiness` | read | An account can trade now, or cannot any more |
| `stream.status` | read | A broker price feed went `up`, `stale` or `down` |
| `safety.kill_switch` | read | The kill switch was turned on or off |
| `safety.limit` | read | A daily safety limit was reached |
| `limits.throttled` | read | A request was slowed by a rate limit |
| `download.progress` | read | A data download moved forward (at most once a second per job) |
| `download.done` | read | A data download finished |
| `download.failed` | read | A data download stopped with an error |
| `collection.changed` | read | A named list of instruments or an option universe was created, changed or deleted |
| `recording.started` | read | A recording started writing |
| `recording.stopped` | read | A recording stopped |
| `recording.gap` | read | A recording missed data because the feed or the login was missing |
| `recording.disk_low` | read | A recording is close to its disk limit |
| `ticket.prepared` | admin | An order waits for a person to approve it on this computer. Carries no approval token |
| `ticket.confirmed` | admin | A person approved an order ticket |
| `ticket.rejected` | admin | A person declined an order ticket |
| `hook.rejected` | admin | A webhook alert was accepted but did not become an order |
| `hook.stale` | admin | A webhook alert was too old to trade on |
| `hook.failed` | admin | An accepted webhook alert's order could not be made |
| `backup.completed` | admin | A backup was written |
| `backup.failed` | admin | A backup could not be written |
| `config.warning` | admin | The Bridge found something in the config worth fixing |

Never offered: `tick` (use the price stream), key events and the audit log. Before an event leaves the Bridge, every field that
looks like a secret, a token, a key, a password or an approval is removed, and key-like text is masked.

## Webhooks: the Bridge calls you

A webhook subscription tells the Bridge: "POST these topics to this URL, signed". Creating one sends data to an outside
address, so it is **this-computer-only** and needs an admin key.

```bash
# the CLI makes a random signing secret and prints it once
mc-bridge subscriptions add https://example.com/bridge/events --topics order.*,download.* --label "my server"
mc-bridge subscriptions test sub_abcdefgh
```

Or with HTTP (the secret is yours to choose, 16 to 256 characters; it is stored encrypted and never returned):

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/subscriptions -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"https://example.com/bridge/events","topics":["order.*","download.*"],"secret":"'"$(openssl rand -hex 32)"'"}'
```

Other commands: `subscriptions list | show | pause | resume | remove | rotate-secret | deliveries | dead-letters | tail`
(`mc-bridge --help`), and `PATCH`, `DELETE /v1/subscriptions/{id}` over HTTP.

### What your server receives

A `POST` with a JSON body (the same envelope as the stream) and these headers:

| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `X-Bridge-Signature` | `v1=<hex>`: HMAC-SHA256 of `<timestamp>.<raw body>` with your secret |
| `X-Bridge-Timestamp` | Whole seconds since 1970 when this attempt was signed |
| `X-Bridge-Event-Id` | The event's cursor. **De-duplicate on it**: delivery is at least once |
| `X-Bridge-Event-Topic` | The topic |
| `X-Bridge-Delivery` | This delivery's id (the same on every retry) |
| `X-Bridge-Attempt` | 1 for the first try, 2 for the next, ... |

Answer with any `2xx` quickly. The answer's body is ignored. Anything else is a failure (see retries).

### Check the signature

Always check it, on the **raw** body (before JSON parsing), and refuse a timestamp more than 5 minutes (300 seconds, set by
`events.webhooks.replayWindowSec`) from your own clock, so a captured request cannot be sent again later. These three
snippets are run by the Bridge's tests against the real signer, so they are checked, not just shown.

Node (no packages):

<!-- snippet:node -->
```js
// verify.js: check a Bridge webhook. Call verify() with the RAW body, not the parsed JSON.
const crypto = require("node:crypto");

function verify({ secret, timestamp, signature, rawBody, toleranceSec = 300 }) {
  if (!timestamp || !signature || !/^\d{1,12}$/.test(timestamp)) return false;
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(timestamp)) > toleranceSec) return false; // too old, or from the future
  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.`).update(rawBody).digest("hex");
  const want = Buffer.from(expected, "hex");
  // the header may hold several signatures ("v1=aaa v1=bbb") while a secret is being replaced
  return signature.split(/[\s,]+/).some((part) => {
    const m = /^v1=([0-9a-f]{64})$/i.exec(part);
    return m !== null && crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(m[1], "hex"), want);
  });
}

module.exports = { verify };
```

A complete receiver with the same check (plain `node:http`; give it the secret in the environment):

<!-- snippet:node-server -->
```js
// receiver.js: node receiver.js   (SECRET=... PORT=8080)
const http = require("node:http");
const { verify } = require("./verify");

const seen = new Set(); // event ids already handled: delivery is at least once

http
  .createServer((req, res) => {
    const chunks = [];
    req.on("data", (c) => chunks.push(c));
    req.on("end", () => {
      const rawBody = Buffer.concat(chunks);
      const ok = verify({ secret: process.env.SECRET, timestamp: req.headers["x-bridge-timestamp"], signature: req.headers["x-bridge-signature"], rawBody });
      if (!ok) return res.writeHead(401).end();
      const eventId = req.headers["x-bridge-event-id"];
      if (!seen.has(eventId)) {
        seen.add(eventId);
        const event = JSON.parse(rawBody.toString("utf8"));
        console.log(event.topic, event.data);
      }
      res.writeHead(204).end();
    });
  })
  .listen(Number(process.env.PORT || 8080), () => console.log("listening"));
```

Python (standard library only):

<!-- snippet:python -->
```python
# verify.py: check a Bridge webhook. Pass the RAW body bytes, not parsed JSON.
import hashlib
import hmac
import re
import time


def verify(secret: str, timestamp: str, signature: str, raw_body: bytes, tolerance_sec: int = 300, now: float = None) -> bool:
    if not timestamp or not signature or not re.fullmatch(r"\d{1,12}", timestamp):
        return False
    if abs((time.time() if now is None else now) - int(timestamp)) > tolerance_sec:
        return False  # too old, or from the future
    expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), timestamp.encode() + b"." + raw_body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    # the header may hold several signatures ("v1=aaa v1=bbb") while a secret is being replaced
    for part in re.split(r"[\s,]+", signature):
        m = re.fullmatch(r"v1=([0-9a-fA-F]{64})", part)
        if m and hmac.compare_digest(m.group(1).lower(), expected):
            return True
    return False
```

In a web framework, take the raw bytes the framework gives you (`request.get_data()` in Flask, `await request.body()` in
FastAPI), and the headers `X-Bridge-Timestamp` and `X-Bridge-Signature`.

Shell (needs `openssl`; good for scripts and for checking by hand):

<!-- snippet:shell -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# verify-bridge-signature.sh <secret> <timestamp> <signature header> <body file>
# exit 0: genuine, exit 1: not. The body file must hold the raw body exactly as received.
set -u
secret="$1"; timestamp="$2"; header="$3"; body_file="$4"
[[ "$timestamp" =~ ^[0-9]{1,12}$ ]] || exit 1
now=$(date +%s)
diff=$(( now - timestamp )); (( diff < 0 )) && diff=$(( -diff ))
(( diff <= ${TOLERANCE_SEC:-300} )) || exit 1
expected=$( { printf '%s.' "$timestamp"; cat "$body_file"; } | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$secret" -hex | sed 's/^.* //' )
for part in ${header//,/ }; do
  [[ "$part" == "v1=$expected" ]] && exit 0
done
exit 1
```

The shell version compares with `[[ == ]]`, which is not constant-time, and `openssl -hmac` puts the secret in the process
list while it runs: fine on your own computer, not for a shared server. Use the Node or Python version there.

### Retries, dead letters and the log

Each event is written to disk before the first attempt, so a restart does not lose it. An attempt that was running when
the Bridge stopped is sent again after the restart.

| Answer | What happens |
|---|---|
| `2xx` | Delivered |
| `5xx`, `408`, `425`, `429`, a timeout, no connection | Retried after 5 s, then 10 s, 20 s ... doubling up to 1 hour, with 20 % jitter; a `Retry-After` is honoured up to that hour. Up to 8 attempts or 24 hours, then a dead letter |
| Other `4xx`, a redirect, a refused target | A dead letter at once: sending it again cannot help |

- **Dead letters**: `GET /v1/subscriptions/{id}/dead-letters`, or `mc-bridge subscriptions dead-letters <id>`. Fix the cause,
  then send them again (`--retry-all`) or forget them (`--clear`). Each subscription keeps at most 500 waiting events; when
  the queue is full the oldest is set aside as a dead letter with the reason `overflow`.
- **Delivery log**: `GET /v1/subscriptions/{id}/deliveries` lists every attempt: time, outcome, HTTP status, a short code
  (`http_5xx`, `timeout`, `tls_failed`, `blocked_address` ...) and how long it took. It never holds your server's answer text,
  the URL's path or the secret.
- **Test**: `POST /v1/subscriptions/{id}/test` (or `subscriptions test <id>`) sends one signed `subscription.test` event now. It is
  not queued and not retried.
- **Order**: events can arrive out of order when a retry overtakes a newer one. Order by the event id.

### Where a webhook may point

The Bridge sits inside your home or office network, so a webhook target is checked hard. It is checked when you save it, and
again before every delivery on the addresses the name points to at that moment:

- `https://` only, no user name or password in the URL, no `localhost` or local-network names (`.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`).
- Every address the host resolves to must be public: never loopback, private (`10.x`, `172.16-31.x`, `192.168.x`),
  link-local (`169.254.x`, `fe80::`), carrier-grade NAT, multicast or reserved. One bad address in the answer refuses the
  delivery. The connection then goes to the address that was checked, not to a second lookup.
- Cloud metadata addresses (`169.254.169.254`, `100.100.100.200`, `168.63.129.16`, `fd00:ec2::254`) are refused **always**.
- The Bridge never follows a redirect, verifies the receiver's certificate every time, gives up after `timeoutMs` (10 s), reads
  at most 4 KB of the answer and throws it away.
- Sending to your own computer or network (a receiver on `127.0.0.1` or a LAN address, plain `http://`) needs
  `events.webhooks.allowPrivateTargets: true` in the config file. It cannot be switched on over HTTP. `allowedHosts` can limit
  targets to a list of hosts.

### The secret

The signing secret is write-only. It is stored encrypted (the secrets store, with your broker credentials) and not in any file of
the events folder, so a backup of the data folder carries no webhook secret. It is never returned by any route, never written to
the log, the delivery log or the audit log. To replace it: `mc-bridge subscriptions rotate-secret <id>` (or `PATCH` with a new
`secret`); update your receiver first, or accept both signatures for a short while (the header can carry several `v1=` values
and the snippets above check each one).

## Settings

`events` in `bridge.config.json` (all optional):

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | Off: no event log, no streams, no webhooks |
| `retain` | `5000` | Events kept for replay, also across a restart |
| `maxEventBytes` | `16384` | An event's data above this is replaced by a short note |
| `heartbeatMs` | `15000` | Keep-alive for streams; also when a revoked key is noticed |
| `maxClients`, `maxClientsPerKey` | `50`, `5` | Open stream connections |
| `maxBufferedBytes` | `262144` | A reader this far behind is closed (`go_away` `slow_consumer`); it reconnects with its cursor |
| `webhooks.enabled` | `true` | |
| `webhooks.maxSubscriptions` | `20` | |
| `webhooks.allowPrivateTargets` | `false` | Let targets be `http://` or on this computer or network (metadata addresses stay refused) |
| `webhooks.allowedHosts` | `[]` | When not empty, targets must match one: `example.com` or `*.example.com` |
| `webhooks.timeoutMs`, `maxResponseBytes`, `concurrency` | `10000`, `4096`, `4` | |
| `webhooks.replayWindowSec` | `300` | What receivers should accept |
| `webhooks.retry` | `maxAttempts 8, baseMs 5000, maxMs 3600000, jitter 0.2, maxAgeSec 86400` | |
| `webhooks.maxPendingPerSubscription`, `deadLetterMax`, `deliveryLogMax` | `500`, `200`, `500` | |

## Troubleshooting

| You see | Do this |
|---|---|
| `401` on the stream | The token is single use and lasts 60 seconds: get a new one, or send an `Authorization` header |
| `gap: true` in `ready` | You were away longer than the Bridge keeps events: read orders and positions from the API, then continue from `cursor` |
| The webhook test says `blocked_address` | The host resolves to a private or metadata address. Use a public host, or `allowPrivateTargets` for a receiver of your own |
| `http_4xx` | Your server refused it: check the signature check, the URL and that you read the **raw** body |
| Signatures never match | The body was parsed and re-written before checking; the secret has a trailing newline; or the two clocks differ by more than 5 minutes |
| A subscription says `needs-secret` | Its stored URL and signing secret are gone (demo mode keeps secrets in memory only, so a restart loses them). Send both again with `PATCH /v1/subscriptions/{id}` (`url` and `secret`), then `subscriptions dead-letters <id> --retry-all`; or remove it and add it again |
| Events stopped for a subscription | `mc-bridge subscriptions list`: is it `paused` or `failing`? Look at `deliveries` and `dead-letters` |

---

<!-- docs/guides/webhooks.md -->

# Alerts: TradingView, signed generic hooks, ChartInk and GoCharting

An alert from your own code or a charting site becomes an order through a **hook**: a URL with a secret token, tied
to one account and a set of limits. Every signal goes through the same safety checks, rate limits, idempotency and
audit log as an order sent from a script. Hooks are **paper** by default.

Four sources are supported:

| Source | Sender | Credential |
|---|---|---|
| `tradingview` | TradingView alerts | URL token **plus** a passphrase inside the alert message (TradingView cannot sign) |
| `generic` | Your own scripts, bots and services | URL token **plus** an HMAC signature on every request |
| `chartink` | ChartInk scan alerts | URL token only (ChartInk cannot sign) |
| `gocharting` | GoCharting alerts | URL token only (GoCharting cannot sign) |

The dashboard does the same as the API below: **Integrations → Webhooks → Create webhook** (choose the source there;
it defaults to TradingView). For TradingView alerts go to [TradingView](#tradingview); the rest of this page covers
every source.

## TradingView

A TradingView alert can place a **paper** order through a `tradingview` hook. TradingView cannot sign a request, so the
hook is protected by three things together: the secret address, a **passphrase** written inside the alert message, and
(optionally) TradingView's published sender addresses. Alerts older than a limit you set are refused, a repeat of an
alert is never placed twice, and nothing the alert says can make the Bridge do more than the hook allows.

### What TradingView does (checked against TradingView's own pages)

Checked on **2026-11-09**. TradingView can change any of this; the Bridge does not depend on the items marked "not
documented".

| Fact | What TradingView says | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Two-step sign-in | Webhook alerts are only allowed when 2-factor authentication is enabled on your TradingView account | [About webhooks](https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000529348-about-webhooks/) |
| Plan | The help page does not name a plan. TradingView's pricing page lists webhook notifications as a feature of its paid plans (not verified here which plan from which tier: check the pricing page for your account) | [Pricing](https://www.tradingview.com/pricing/) |
| Ports | Only ports 80 and 443 are accepted; other ports are rejected | About webhooks |
| Time allowed | If the server takes longer than **three seconds**, the request is cancelled | About webhooks |
| Retries | **Not documented.** The page says a webhook may occasionally fail to arrive and points to the alert log's "Webhook status" column. Assume TradingView does not resend: the Bridge answers at once and never relies on a resend | About webhooks |
| Message and content type | The alert message is the request body. If it is valid JSON, TradingView sends `Content-Type: application/json`; otherwise `text/plain` | About webhooks |
| Headers and signing | The help page describes no way to add a header or sign the request. The Bridge therefore uses a passphrase inside the message | About webhooks |
| Sender addresses | 52.89.214.238, 34.212.75.30, 54.218.53.128, 52.32.178.7 | About webhooks |
| IPv6 | Not supported for webhooks | About webhooks |
| Time placeholders | `{{timenow}}` is the moment the alert fires, `{{time}}` the start of the bar; both are UTC, written like `2019-08-27T09:56:00Z`, to the nearest second | [Variables in alerts](https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000531021-how-to-use-a-variable-value-in-alert/) |
| Other placeholders | `{{ticker}}`, `{{exchange}}`, `{{close}}`, `{{interval}}`; for strategies `{{strategy.order.action}}` (buy or sell), `{{strategy.order.contracts}}`, `{{strategy.order.price}}`, `{{strategy.order.id}}`, `{{strategy.market_position}}` (long, flat or short), `{{strategy.market_position_size}}` (never negative) | Variables in alerts |
| Placeholders in Pine | In Pine's `alert()` the message is plain text you build yourself with `str.tostring()`; placeholders work in the alert dialog's Message box, not inside `alert()` or a strategy's `alert_message` | [Pine alerts](https://www.tradingview.com/pine-script-docs/concepts/alerts/) |
| Not documented | Message size limit, whether redirects are followed, the User-Agent, how the reply body is used | |

What the Bridge does about the gaps: it accepts a body of up to 16 KB, answers `202` within milliseconds (well inside
three seconds), and treats an identical alert it has already seen as a duplicate, so a resend, if TradingView ever
sends one, cannot place a second order.

### Set it up

1. **Make the hook.** Dashboard: API, Integrations, Webhooks, choose **TradingView**, then **Create webhook**. Copy the
   **webhook address** and the **passphrase** now; the Bridge keeps only a fingerprint of each and cannot show them
   again. (The same from the API: `POST /v1/hooks` with `"source": "tradingview"`.)
2. **Give TradingView an address on the internet.** `http://127.0.0.1:4300/...` only works on this computer. Follow
   [Exposing alerts safely](expose-alerts.md); you end with an address like `https://alerts.example.com`. Type it into
   the dashboard form (or the box under the new hook) and it shows the final address to paste. The final address is
   that address followed by the hook's path: `https://alerts.example.com/hooks/tradingview/<token>`. It must use port
   80 or 443.
3. **Create the alert in TradingView.** Open a chart, then the alarm-clock icon (or Alt+A).
   - Choose the condition (an indicator, a strategy, or a price level).
   - Notifications tab: tick **Webhook URL** and paste the address.
   - Settings tab: replace the whole **Message** box with one of the messages below, with your passphrase in it.
   - Create the alert.
4. **Check it.** In the dashboard, open **Alerts** on the hook and choose **Send a test alert**: the Bridge runs a
   realistic alert through the same checks and places a paper order. A test proves the hook works; it does not prove that
   TradingView can reach it. When a real alert fires, it appears in the same list within seconds. Hooks that have never
   heard anything, or have been quiet for days, say so there.

### The alert message

JSON is easiest. Numbers such as `{{close}}` stay **without quotes**; text placeholders have quotes. TradingView fills
the placeholders in, then sends the result as JSON.

**Indicator or price alert:**

```
{
  "symbol": "{{exchange}}:{{ticker}}",
  "side": "buy",
  "lots": 1,
  "orderType": "limit",
  "price": {{close}},
  "product": "MIS",
  "mode": "paper",
  "id": "my-alert",
  "time": "{{timenow}}",
  "passphrase": "YOUR_PASSPHRASE"
}
```

**Strategy alert** (every order fill; TradingView fills in the action, size, price and position):

```
{
  "symbol": "{{exchange}}:{{ticker}}",
  "side": "{{strategy.order.action}}",
  "lots": {{strategy.order.contracts}},
  "orderType": "limit",
  "price": {{strategy.order.price}},
  "product": "MIS",
  "mode": "paper",
  "marketPosition": "{{strategy.market_position}}",
  "positionSize": {{strategy.market_position_size}},
  "id": "{{strategy.order.id}}",
  "time": "{{timenow}}",
  "passphrase": "YOUR_PASSPHRASE"
}
```

**Plain text** also works (TradingView then sends `text/plain`): one order, side first, then the symbol and size, then
the rest in any order:

```
BUY {{exchange}}:{{ticker}} 1 @ {{close}} MIS mode=paper id=my-alert time={{timenow}} passphrase=YOUR_PASSPHRASE
```

The dashboard prints these with your real passphrase and your hook's order type and product already filled in
(`MARKET` hooks leave out `price`; a hook that fixes the product leaves out `product`).

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `symbol` | The chart ticker with its exchange, `{{exchange}}:{{ticker}}`. A name with no exchange is refused: the same name can exist on two exchanges, and the Bridge never guesses |
| `side` | `buy` or `sell` (not `long`, `short` or `exit`). Left out only when the hook fixes the side |
| `lots` or `quantity` | Not both. For futures and options `{{strategy.order.contracts}}` counts lots, so send it as `lots`. For shares, 1 lot is 1 share. If both are left out the order is one lot |
| `orderType` | `limit` or `market`; must match the hook. A LIMIT hook needs `price` |
| `product` | `CNC`, `INTRADAY`, `MARGIN`, or the broker words `MIS` (INTRADAY), `NRML` (MARGIN), `DELIVERY`, `CARRYFORWARD`. If the hook fixes a product, a different one is refused |
| `account` | Optional. Must be the hook's own account |
| `mode` | `paper` (the default when left out) or `live`. Must equal the hook's mode |
| `marketPosition`, `positionSize` | Strategy alerts. Recorded with the alert and shown in the list; the order is the buy or sell TradingView sent. The Bridge does not net positions in this version |
| `time` | `{{timenow}}`. Used for the age limit and as part of the alert's identity. Required on a live hook |
| `id` | Your alert's name or `{{strategy.order.id}}`. With `time`, `symbol` and `side` it is the alert's identity |
| `passphrase` | The hook's passphrase, in the message. Never shown again, never logged |

Any other field refuses the alert (`quantiy` is refused, not read as a one-lot order). So does an unfilled
`{{placeholder}}`, a bad number, or JSON that is not valid JSON (the reply names what is wrong).

**Pine `alert()` (indicator).** Placeholders do not work inside `alert()`: build the text yourself with
`str.tostring()`, as below. Test the time format in the Pine Editor before relying on it.

```pine
//@version=6
indicator("Breakout alert", overlay = true)
breakout = ta.crossover(close, ta.sma(close, 20))
nowUtc = str.format_time(timenow, "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss", "UTC") + "Z"
if breakout
    alert('{"symbol": "' + syminfo.prefix + ':' + syminfo.ticker + '", "side": "buy", "lots": 1, "orderType": "limit", "price": ' + str.tostring(close) + ', "product": "MIS", "mode": "paper", "id": "breakout", "time": "' + nowUtc + '", "passphrase": "YOUR_PASSPHRASE"}', alert.freq_once_per_bar_close)
```

**Pine strategy.** The simplest way is the strategy template above in the alert's Message box (placeholders work there).
To send different text per order, give the order an `alert_message` and put `{{strategy.order.alert_message}}` in the
Message box; the text in `alert_message` is built in Pine like the indicator example, and an order without one sends an
empty message (which the Bridge refuses with a clear reason).

### Names: chart tickers, products

The Bridge reads the alert's symbol the way a chart writes it (the `from=chart` mapping) and refuses anything it cannot
map to exactly one instrument.

| In TradingView | Bridge symbol | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `NSE:RELIANCE` | `NSE:RELIANCE` | cash |
| `NSE:M_M`, `NSE:BAJAJ_AUTO` | `NSE:M&M`, `NSE:BAJAJ-AUTO` | charts write `_` where the exchange writes `&` or `-` |
| `NSE:NIFTY1!`, `NSE:NIFTY2!` | the nearest and the next NIFTY future (`NFO:NIFTY-...-FUT`) | resolved from the instrument master when the alert arrives; quantity must be a multiple of the lot size, so send `lots` |
| `NSE:NIFTY261027C25000` | `NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-25000-CE` | option written as YYMMDD, C or P, strike (the Bridge's reading of the chart form; check it with a test alert on your symbol) |
| `NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-FUT` | unchanged | a full Bridge symbol is accepted as is |
| `RELIANCE` (no exchange) | refused | send `{{exchange}}:{{ticker}}` |
| `NSE:NIFTY` | refused when the order is placed | an index cannot be traded |

Products: `MIS` = `INTRADAY`, `NRML` = `MARGIN`, `CNC` = delivery. An unknown ticker is accepted by the receiver and then
**rejected after the 202** (`SYMBOL_NOT_FOUND`); it shows in the hook's Alerts list with the reason.

A continuous future (`NIFTY1!`) rolls to a new contract at expiry; a hook with `allowedSymbols` lists exact contracts and
must be updated at each roll (the create response warns 7 days ahead).

### What protects a TradingView hook

| Protection | What it does |
|---|---|
| Secret address | A 256-bit token in the URL; only its hash is stored |
| Passphrase | In the message; 128 random bits, shown once, stored hashed, compared in constant time. A wrong one is `401`; 30 wrong ones a minute from one address answer `429` |
| Sender addresses | `"sourceIpPreset": "tradingview"` accepts only the four TradingView addresses above, plus any in `allowSourceIps` and the global `hooks.allowSourceIps`. Behind a tunnel the Bridge sees the tunnel, not TradingView: set `hooks.clientIpHeader` (`cf-connecting-ip` for Cloudflare Tunnel; trusted only when the connection comes from this computer) or every alert is refused |
| Age limit | `maxAgeSec` (default 120): an alert whose `time` is older is refused as stale, one more than a minute in the future too. If fresh alerts are refused, check this computer's clock |
| No double orders | An alert is identified by `id` + `time` + `symbol` + `side`: a resend is acknowledged as a duplicate and places nothing. The memory is a small file in your data folder (`hooks-seen.json`, bounded, hashes only), so a restart does not forget. The order itself carries a derived `clientOrderId` (`mcb-<hook>-<hash>`) and a stable Idempotency-Key, so even a lost memory cannot place the same alert twice that day |
| Burst of alerts | Orders are paced by the account's order-rate cap. An alert that meets it waits (queued, up to `hooks.burstWaitSec`, 30 by default) and is placed when a slot frees up, instead of being refused; past that wait, or when the queue (`hooks.queueSize`) is full, it is refused with a clear reason and nothing is placed |
| The hook's own limits | Account, allowed symbols, lots cap, product, order type and side are fixed on the hook; everything else is refused, never trimmed |
| Paper first | Alerts are paper unless the hook is live. A paper hook refuses an alert that says `"mode": "live"` |

**Live TradingView hooks.** Everything above, plus: creating one needs the `live` scope, live enabled for the account in
the config, and one of `sourceIpPreset`/`allowSourceIps`, `requireConfirmation` or `acknowledgeUnsignedLive`; it must
have `maxAgeSec`; every alert must say `"mode": "live"` and carry its `time`; and the key that created it must still
exist. An alert without `"mode": "live"` means paper, so a live hook refuses it. With `requireConfirmation` the alert
only opens a ticket that you confirm on this computer. A test alert is always a paper order.

### Where to look when it does not work

Dashboard: **API, Integrations, Webhooks, Alerts** on the hook. Every alert that reached the hook is there with what
happened to it; wrong passphrases and refused addresses are counted at the top. The same from the API:
`GET /v1/hooks/{hookId}/signals`. The audit log (`hook.signal`, `hook.refused`) keeps the permanent record.

| What you see | Likely cause and what to do |
|---|---|
| Nothing in Alerts, and TradingView's alert log says it fired | The alert never reached the Bridge. Check the address in the alert's Webhook URL box (the path must include `/hooks/tradingview/`), that the tunnel is running and `server.publicIngress.allowedHosts` has its host, that the port is 80 or 443, and TradingView's own "Webhook status" in its alert log. Try the test alert, then `curl` the address from another network |
| "1 wrong passphrase" counted | The message has no passphrase or the wrong one. Copy the message again from the dashboard |
| "from an address that is not allowed" counted | You turned on the TradingView address list and the Bridge sees another address. Behind a tunnel set `hooks.clientIpHeader`; if TradingView changed its addresses, edit `hooks.presets.tradingview` |
| Unreadable | The reason says what: an unfilled `{{placeholder}}` (the placeholder is in a place TradingView does not fill, for example a strategy placeholder in a plain alert), invalid JSON (quote text placeholders, leave numbers bare), an unknown field, a missing exchange |
| Too old | The alert's `time` is older than `maxAgeSec`. Use `{{timenow}}`, not `{{time}}` (the bar's start). If every alert is too old, check this computer's clock |
| Not placed, reason shown | The alert arrived and the order was refused: an unknown symbol, over the lots cap, the product or order type differs from the hook, a limit price too far from the market, the kill switch, a closed market, the account cannot trade. Nothing was placed |
| Placed but you expected a live order | The hook is paper. Alerts on a paper hook never place live orders |
| Needs you | The hook requires confirmation: confirm the ticket in the dashboard (Orders, Pending confirmations) within a minute |
| TradingView says the alert timed out | The Bridge answers in milliseconds, so the delay is the tunnel or the network. Do not resend by hand: check the Alerts list first; if it arrived, it is there |

A rejected order after the `202` is announced on the Bridge's event bus as `hook.rejected` (a notifier such as Telegram
can deliver it), and is in the audit log. Wrong passphrases and refused addresses are counted and audited (at most
once a minute per hook), never announced.

### Settings for TradingView hooks

Per hook (`POST /v1/hooks`): `source: "tradingview"`, `maxAgeSec` (5 to 3600, default 120), `sourceIpPreset`
(`"tradingview"`). In the config file, section `hooks`:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `clientIpHeader` | `null` | Header that carries the real sender address behind a local tunnel |
| `presets.tradingview` | built in | `{ "ips": [...], "verifiedAt": "2026-11-09", "source": "https://..." }`: the address list, shown in the dashboard and by `GET /v1/hooks/presets`; edit it when TradingView's page changes |
| `burstWaitSec` | `30` | How long an alert may wait for an order-rate slot; `0` turns waiting off |
| `signalsKept` | `100` | Alerts remembered per hook for the Alerts list (memory only) |
| `dedupeWindowMs`, `queueSize`, `maxSignalsPerMinute` | as in the config reference | |


## 1. Create a hook

Admin key, from this computer:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/hooks -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "source": "generic",
  "label": "NIFTY breakout",
  "account": "paper",
  "mode": "paper",
  "product": "MARGIN",
  "orderType": "LIMIT",
  "maxLotsPerSignal": 2,
  "allowedSymbols": ["NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-FUT"],
  "requireConfirmation": false
}'
```

The reply holds `url` and `path` (with the token; **shown once**, only a hash is kept), for `generic` hooks a
`signingSecret` and for `tradingview` hooks a `passphrase` (also shown once), ready-to-paste `templates` for the alert message, and any `warnings`. `GET /v1/hooks` lists hooks without tokens; `DELETE /v1/hooks/{hookId}`
stops a URL at once.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `source` | `tradingview`, `generic`, `chartink` or `gocharting` |
| `account` | The account orders go to |
| `mode` | `paper` (default) or `live`. Creating a live hook is refused unless the creating key has the `live` scope as well as `admin`, the account has `live.enabled` and `"webhook"` in its `live.allowedSources`, `safety.liveTrading` is on, and (for unsigned sources, see below) one of `allowSourceIps`, `requireConfirmation` or `acknowledgeUnsignedLive` is set |
| `side` | Fix the side (`BUY`/`SELL`). Required for ChartInk, whose alerts carry none; otherwise an alert asking for the other side is refused |
| `product`, `orderType` | Fixed per hook (`LIMIT` alerts must carry a price) |
| `maxLotsPerSignal` | Larger signals are refused, never trimmed |
| `allowedSymbols` | Only these canonical symbols (recommended for derivatives). Exact contracts: a dated future stops matching on expiry, so the create response warns 7 days ahead; update the hook at each roll-over |
| `requireConfirmation` | Every signal waits on the dashboard (Pending confirmations); confirming places exactly that order, once; declining ends the signal as `rejected` (`TICKET_REJECTED`) and nothing is sent |
| `allowSourceIps` | Optional allowlist of sender IP addresses or IPv4 CIDR blocks (for example the addresses your alert service publishes) |
| `sourceIpPreset` | `"tradingview"`: also accept alerts only from TradingView's published addresses (the editable list in the config, see [TradingView](#tradingview)) |
| `maxAgeSec` | Refuse an alert whose own `time` is older than this many seconds (5 to 3600). TradingView hooks default to 120 and a live one must have it; for other sources it applies when the alert carries a `time` written like `2026-11-09T09:56:00Z` |
| `acknowledgeUnsignedLive` | `true` to accept that a live ChartInk, GoCharting or TradingView hook is protected by its URL (and passphrase) alone (audited and shown on the hook) |

**Unsigned live hooks: the trade-off.** ChartInk, GoCharting and TradingView cannot sign their alerts, so the URL
token is the only credential, and that URL lives in your charting account, browser history and tunnel logs. Replay
protection is only the dedupe window. For `"mode": "live"` the Bridge therefore insists on at least one extra guard:
`allowSourceIps` or `sourceIpPreset` (best, when the service publishes its sending addresses), `requireConfirmation: true` (you approve each
order), or an explicit `acknowledgeUnsignedLive: true`. Signed `generic` hooks (HMAC with a timestamp) need none of
these. The key that created a live hook is recorded on it; revoke that key and the hook stops accepting alerts.

## 2. Make the URL reachable

TradingView, ChartInk and GoCharting post from the internet (TradingView only to port 80 or 443), and so does any script running
elsewhere. The full walk-through, with a safe tunnel, is [Exposing alerts safely](expose-alerts.md); in short: Turn on the **public ingress** listener, which serves `/hooks/*` and nothing else, and run your own tunnel
to it:

```json
"server": { "publicIngress": { "enabled": true, "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 4301, "allowedHosts": ["hooks.example.com"] } }
```

```bash
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:4301     # or a named tunnel with your own host name
```

`mc-bridge expose alerts` does this (and the host list, the client-address header and a TradingView sender allowlist) in one
step and checks the result: see [expose-alerts.md](expose-alerts.md).

Give the sender `https://<tunnel host>/hooks/<source>/<token>` (the `path` from step 1). If the tunnel runs on this
computer and adds a client-IP header, set `hooks.clientIpHeader` so IP allowlists see the real sender (trusted only from loopback).

## 3. Alert messages

### Signed generic hook (your own code)

The recommended source for anything you control.

`"source": "generic"` returns a `signingSecret` (shown once). Sign each request:

```python
import hmac, hashlib, json, time, urllib.request

body = json.dumps({"symbol": "NSE:RELIANCE", "side": "BUY", "quantity": 1, "orderType": "MARKET", "id": "sig-42"}).encode()
t = str(int(time.time()))
sig = hmac.new(SECRET.encode(), t.encode() + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
req = urllib.request.Request(HOOK_URL, data=body, method="POST",
                             headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-MCB-Signature": f"t={t},v1={sig}"})
print(urllib.request.urlopen(req).read())
```

Requests older or newer than 5 minutes, or replayed inside that window, are refused with `401` before the body is
read. `{ "signals": [...], "id": "batch-7" }` sends several at once.

The body accepts `symbol` (any symbol the Bridge understands, canonical preferred), `side`, `quantity` or `lots`,
`price` (required for `LIMIT` hooks), `orderType`, `product`, and `id` (+ optional `time`). Reusing an `id` the same
day never creates a second order. When the body also carries `time`, the identity is `id` **and** `time`: a sender that
reuses one id every day (a strategy order id such as `Long`) still gets a new order for each new time.

### ChartInk

Create the hook with `"source": "chartink"` and a fixed `"side"`. Paste the URL into the scan's webhook box. ChartInk
sends its standard JSON (`stocks`, `trigger_prices`, `triggered_at`, `scan_name`); each stock becomes one signal of one
lot (one share for cash) at most, up to the per-alert cap.

### GoCharting

`"source": "gocharting"`; the alert text uses the plain-text grammar, for example `SELL NSE:SBIN 5 MKT INTRADAY` or
`BUY NSE:RELIANCE 10 @ 1402.5 id=L1 time=2026-10-19T04:00:00Z`. A JSON message works too. When the message carries
both `id` and `time`, a double delivery (or a re-delivery the same day) places **one** order; otherwise identical
messages inside `hooks.dedupeWindowMs` count as one. Words the Bridge does not understand, or an unfilled
`{{placeholder}}`, refuse the alert instead of guessing. Use `allowedSymbols` on derivative hooks.

## 4. What happens to a signal

`queued` → `processing` → `placed` | `duplicate` | `awaiting_confirmation` | `rejected` | `failed` |
`outcome_unknown`. Each step is in the audit log as `hook.signal` with the hook id, symbol, order id and reason. A
full queue answers `429` with a message that says so (never unbounded); each hook is limited to
`hooks.maxSignalsPerMinute`. The kill switch refuses every signal. An order that meets the account's order-rate cap
waits for a free slot (`hooks.burstWaitSec`) instead of being refused.

`GET /v1/hooks/{hookId}/signals` lists the recent alerts of a hook (newest first, at most `hooks.signalsKept`, memory
only) with an `outcome` (`placed`, `queued`, `awaiting_confirmation`, `duplicate`, `stale`, `rejected`, `refused`,
`failed`, `outcome_unknown`, `dropped`), a plain-words `summary`, the reason and the order id, plus counts that also
include wrong passphrases and refused addresses (counted, never listed, never with a body).
